About the Department

Our story

A volunteer department, formed in 2009, that grew up with its town.

The Triana Volunteer Fire Department was formed on July 23, 2009, as a nonprofit corporation in Madison County, Alabama, to give the Town of Triana a fire department of its own.

Triana sits on the Tennessee River in southern Madison County, and it has grown quickly. The department has grown with it. What started as a founding crew of volunteers now answers hundreds of calls a year: structure and vehicle fires, medical emergencies, rescues, and the service calls in between. In 2025 the department ran 429 calls; the 2026 count passed 350 by mid-October.

Today the department runs out of Station 43 at 465 6th Street, with five paid staff and a roster of volunteers who live in and around the community they serve. Members train to state standards in fire suppression, emergency medical response, and technical rescue, and the department keeps building: recent grant applications seek new turnout gear for six volunteers and updated radios for clearer communication on scene.

The department is governed by a board of directors and led day to day by its fire chief. It is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, which means donations and grants go directly to equipment, training, and readiness.

About the Department

Mission

The purpose the department is organized for, in the words of its bylaws.

From the bylaws · Article I, Section 3

The Department is organized exclusively for charitable and public-safety purposes within the meaning of section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. Its mission is to protect lives, property and the environment through emergency response (fire suppression, emergency medical services, technical rescue), community risk reduction, fire prevention, public education and training.

What that means on the ground

Emergency response is the core: when someone in Triana calls 911 for a fire, a medical emergency, or a rescue, this department answers, around the clock.

Community risk reduction is the work that keeps calls from happening: smoke alarm checks, fire prevention visits, and safety education for schools and neighborhoods.

Training runs both ways. Members train constantly to stay ready, and the department teaches the public, from station tours for schoolchildren to CPR classes for residents.

The full bylaws, revised in April 2026, are posted with the department's other public documents under Board and Meetings.

Join TVFD

Why volunteer

When the tones drop in Triana, the people who answer are the people who live here.

Not everyone runs into a burning building, and the department does not ask everyone to. A volunteer department runs on many kinds of people, and there is a lane for nearly everyone.

Lane 1

Firefighting

Interior and exterior fire attack, ventilation, search, and water supply. The department trains you to the standard and provides your turnout gear, helmet, and breathing apparatus.

Lane 2

EMS and medical response

Most of our calls are medical. EMTs and first responders assess patients, start care, and work alongside the ambulance service. Two-thirds of what this department does happens in living rooms, not firegrounds.

Lane 3

Driving and apparatus

Engines and support vehicles do not drive themselves. Driver-operators get apparatus training and keep the fleet ready to roll, day and night.

Lane 4

Support roles

Fundraising, grant writing, photography, station projects, public events, and the paperwork that keeps a nonprofit running. If you have a skill, the department can almost certainly use it.

What you get back

  • Real training, free. Fire and EMS training that counts, taught to state standards.
  • Your gear, provided. Turnout gear and equipment are the department's cost, not yours.
  • A crew. The people on the truck become the people you call first, on and off calls.
  • A town that knows your name. There is no abstract about it: the next call is a neighbor.

Join TVFD

Requirements and training

What it takes to join, stated plainly, and the training the department puts behind you.

How joining works

Send the interest form

Two minutes, name and contact details. It goes to the chief's inbox, and you will hear back from a person, not a system.

Visit a training night

Come watch the crew train at Station 43 before you commit to anything. Meet the officers, see the apparatus, ask the awkward questions.

Application and conversation

A short application and a sit-down with the chief about which lane fits you and what your schedule can honestly carry.

Train, gear up, respond

You are issued gear, start department training, and begin responding alongside experienced members. Nobody runs a call alone before they are ready.

The honest expectations

  • Time: training nights are the backbone, plus the calls you are available for. Volunteers respond from home, so availability is flexible, but training is not optional.
  • Fitness: firefighting is physical work. EMS and support lanes carry their own demands and are open to people who cannot do interior fire attack.
  • Standards: members train to Alabama fire and EMS standards and follow department policy on and off scene.

Training the department provides

New members start with department orientation and basic skills, then progress through firefighter and EMS training as their lane requires. Ongoing training happens at Station 43 on training nights, with regional classes and certifications supported as members advance. The gear on your back and the training behind it are the department's investment in you.

Safety and Prevention

Burning rules

When outdoor burning is allowed around Triana, and when it is not. Read this before you light anything.

The short version: check the conditions before every burn, keep the fire small and attended, and if the wind is up or the woods are dry, do not burn. When in doubt, call the station at (256) 772-2766 and ask.

Before you burn

  • Check for burn restrictions. The Alabama Forestry Commission issues burn permits and can restrict burning during dry or windy periods. State and county rules apply in and around Triana, and permits are required for many kinds of outdoor burning.
  • Watch the weather. Never burn on a windy day, and never burn when a drought or red-flag condition is in effect.
  • Burn only natural material. Yard debris and brush are one thing. Household trash, tires, plastics, and treated lumber are never legal or safe to burn.

While you burn

  • Stay with the fire. An attended fire is a controlled fire. Leaving a burn unattended is how most brush fires start.
  • Keep water close. A connected hose or buckets of water and a shovel, within reach, before the match.
  • Keep it small and contained. A manageable pile, well clear of woods, fences, structures, and power lines.
  • Put it fully out. Cold to the touch before you walk away. Embers can hold heat for hours.

If a fire gets away from you

Call 911 immediately. Do not wait to see if you can handle it: grass and brush fires move faster than people expect, and the sooner we roll, the smaller the fire stays. There is no charge and no trouble for calling early.

Safety and Prevention

Smoke alarms and home safety

Working smoke alarms cut the risk of dying in a home fire roughly in half. Here is how to keep yours working.

The basics

  • Where: inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level of the home.
  • Test monthly: press the button. If it does not sound, change the battery or replace the alarm.
  • Replace at 10 years: alarms wear out even if the test button still chirps. Check the date printed on the back.
  • Never disable one: a chirping alarm needs a battery or a replacement, not a removal. A disconnected alarm protects nobody.

Have a way out

Know two ways out of every room, keep a meeting place outside where everyone gathers, and practice the plan with the whole household twice a year. When an alarm sounds at 3 a.m. is the wrong time to work it out.

Ask us to check

Not sure your alarms are placed right, or need a hand testing or replacing one? Call the station at (256) 772-2766 or send the contact form, and we will set up a home safety visit. It is free, it is quick, and it is exactly the kind of call we would rather get.

A firefighter installing a ceiling smoke alarm. Placeholder photo.

Safety and Prevention

Station tours and visits

School groups, scout troops, birthday kids, and curious neighbors are all welcome at Station 43.

What a visit looks like

Groups tour the station, climb into the apparatus, see a firefighter gear up (so the gear is not scary when it matters), and hear a short, age-right talk on fire safety: what to do when an alarm sounds, and why you never hide from a firefighter.

We come to you, too

Crews visit schools, churches, and community events around Triana with a truck and a safety talk. If your event needs a fire truck and a couple of firefighters, ask early: the calendar fills up in the fall.

How to request

Call the station at (256) 772-2766 or use the contact form with your group, your dates, and roughly how many are coming. One honest note: Station 43 is a working station. If a call comes in during your visit, the crew goes, and that is part of the lesson too.

Families touring an engine at an open house. Placeholder photo.

News and Events

Department news

Grants, equipment, milestones, and the work in between. Short posts, posted as things happen.

October 8, 2026 · Grants

Grant application submitted for new turnout gear

The department has applied to the Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation for six complete LION V-Force turnout sets, $34,968 in all. The sets are for six named volunteers: four who have no structural gear of their own, and two whose sets are more than 15 years old and coming apart. Structural gear has a service life, and past it, it stops protecting the person inside it. This is the department's first application to the foundation; awards are announced in the foundation's quarterly cycle.

Radios

October 17, 2026 · Grants

Radio grant application submitted

The department has submitted an application to the Future is for Everyone Fund, Meta's community fund administered through ChangeX, toward updated portable radios. On a working fire or a highway wreck, a radio that cannot be heard is a safety problem, not an inconvenience. The application was filed ahead of the fund's October 19 deadline.

Community · Classes

Community CPR classes run through the year

Most cardiac arrests happen at home, and the person most likely to be standing there is family. The department teaches community CPR classes at Station 43 through the year, with registration handled online so class sizes stay workable. Watch the events calendar and the department's Facebook page for the next date.

Support the Department

Donate

The Triana Volunteer Fire Department is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Donations are tax-deductible and go to equipment, training, and readiness.

What your money does here

Grants buy the big things, slowly, one application at a time. Donations cover everything in between, right now: the gloves and hoods that wear out, the training props, the small repairs that cannot wait for a funding cycle. When the department applied for six sets of turnout gear this fall, it was because two sets in service are over 15 years old and coming apart. That is the gap your donation closes.

Ways to give

  • By check: payable to Triana Volunteer Fire Department, mailed or brought to Station 43, 465 6th Street, Madison, AL 35756.
  • In person: stop by the station. Someone will put the coffee on.
  • Business support: local businesses sponsor events and equipment through the year; call the station and ask for the chief or the Fundraising Committee.

Online giving is being set up for the new website. Until the button works, the mailbox and the front door do.

Contact

Media and records requests

One front door for reporters, and one for public records.

Media inquiries

Fire Chief Chad Beddingfield is the department's publicity contact. Reporters on a deadline should call the station at (256) 772-2766 and ask for the chief. During a working incident, information comes through the chief or the officer in charge on scene, once the scene allows it.

Public records

Meeting agendas, minutes, bylaws, and the department's formation and tax documents are posted under Board and Meetings, and most requests end there. For anything else, send a written request to the department at 465 6th Street, Madison, AL 35756, or use the contact form and choose "Something else." Say what record you need and how to reach you, and the board secretary will route it.

Incident reports

If you need a report from a call at your own property, contact the station with the date and address. Some records carry privacy limits, and the department will tell you plainly what it can and cannot release.
